results.title: GPU Price Index: Live Rates vs. Public Cloud | Aven Cloud

Every row combines Aven Cloud's live on-demand catalogue price — adjusted continuously to supply and demand — with the public on-demand list price published by each of the three largest public clouds for a comparable GPU. Nothing here is a quote or an estimate: the Aven Cloud side is the exact price you'd pay to order that GPU as of 14 November 2026, 07:59 UTC, and the reference side is a documented, dated list price (see Methodology below).

Per-second billing, no egress fees, release anytime.

### Methodology

Reference prices are the published on-demand list prices of the three largest public clouds: single-GPU instance where offered, otherwise the per-GPU share of the smallest instance carrying that GPU, largest US region, before any discount.

Checked 11 September 2026

...

Each row is one GPU model. On-demand is Aven Cloud's current single-GPU rate, adjusted continuously to supply and demand; spot is the interruptible rate for the same GPU where one is listed, and it can move on every refresh. Public cloud range is the low-to-high published on-demand list price for a comparable single-GPU instance across the three largest public clouds. Savings compares Aven Cloud's on-demand price with the high end of that range — the list price most buyers actually pay before any negotiated discount — and a short sparkline shows how Aven Cloud's own on-demand price has moved over time.

For example, Aven Cloud's current on-demand rate for a single H100 SXM5 is $4.51/GPU-hour, against a public range of $6.90-$12.29 — up to 63% lower than the top of that range. A GPU with no public-cloud reference yet, because it's too new or too specialized for a clean single-GPU match, shows the Aven Cloud price on its own rather than a guessed comparison.

To put that in hours: renting a single H100 SXM5 for 24 hours costs $108.24 on Aven Cloud at the on-demand rate above — up to 63% less than the same 24 hours at the top of the public-cloud range, with no egress fees or minimum term added on top.

...

The aggregate figure at the top of the table is a simple average of the 1-GPU on-demand prices available that day — not weighted by usage, and it can move when a GPU is added to or dropped from the comparison, not only when a price changes. List prices are also not the whole story on either side: a hyperscaler customer with a negotiated enterprise discount or reserved capacity may pay less than the list price shown here, just as an Aven Cloud spot price isn't directly comparable to an on-demand list price. Treat the index as a fair, sourced starting point — not the final word on any one contract.

results.title: Flopper Now Tracks GPU Rental Prices Across 24 Cloud Providers | Flopper.io
highlights:
337 per-GPU hourly rates from 24 clouds, refreshed every six hours, with price history back to July 2026. The spec database now tells you what each accelerator costs to rent, and who is cheapest today.

...

Flopper.io started as a specification database: peak TFLOPS by precision, memory, bandwidth and power for every datacenter GPU. Specs answer half of the buying question. The other half is price, and that number lives on 24 different pricing pages, in 24 different units. As of today, the pricing index collects 337 live listings from 24 GPU cloud providers, covering 89 GPUs, normalized to one unit: US dollars per GPU per hour. The pipeline refreshes every six hours and has recorded every price change since 14 July 2026, so each GPU page now carries a price history alongside its spec sheet.

## What the Same GPU Costs, Cloud to Cloud

The spread is the story. On the day of publication, an on-demand H100 SXM5 80 GB (2022) is listed by 16 providers, and the most expensive listing costs nearly seven times the cheapest. The B200 (2024) shows the same pattern with a three-fold gap across eight clouds. Some of that gap is real: interconnect, storage, support and region all cost money. Some of it is simply price discovery that has not happened yet, because nobody was lining the numbers up.

| GPU | Providers | Cheapest on-demand | Highest on-demand |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80 GB | 16 | $1.79/hr | $12.29/hr |
| NVIDIA A100 SXM4 80 GB | 11 | $1.40/hr | $4.10/hr |
| NVIDIA L40S 48 GB | 11 | $0.87/hr | $2.25/hr |
| NVIDIA H200 SXM 141 GB | 10 | $2.99/hr | $10.60/hr |
| NVIDIA B200 SXM 180 GB | 8 | $4.09/hr | $14.00/hr |
| NVIDIA B300 SXM 288 GB | 6 | $7.40/hr | $11.19/hr |
| AMD Instinct MI300X 192 GB | 5 | $2.39/hr | $6.00/hr |

On-demand, per-GPU, USD, as recorded on 9 September 2026. Spot, community and reserved listings are excluded from the range. Each GPU links to its live pricing page, which will have moved on by the time you read this.

...

Coverage spans three kinds of seller. Hyperscale and general clouds publish rate cards: Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud, DigitalOcean, OVHcloud, Scaleway and Vultr. AI-first clouds, the neoclouds, sell the dense H100, H200 and Blackwell capacity that training runs need: CoreWeave, Lambda Labs, Nebius, Crusoe, DataCrunch, Hyperstack and their peers. Marketplaces, RunPod and Vast.ai, list third-party hosts and set the floor for most consumer and workstation parts.

A listing is one GPU at one pricing type from one provider.

...

No two providers quote the same way. One prices an eight-GPU node, another a single accelerator, a third a monthly contract, and Scaleway prices in euros. Every listing goes through the same four steps before it reaches a page.

- Per GPU, per hour, in USD. Node prices are divided by the GPU count. Monthly rates are divided by 730 hours. Non-USD prices are converted at the live exchange rate on the day of the sync.
- Pricing types are kept apart. On-demand (191 listings), spot or preemptible (31), marketplace community hosts (111) and reserved commitments (4) never share a row. The headline cheapest price on each GPU page is always on-demand, so an interruptible instance cannot masquerade as the market rate.
- Every listing maps to one canonical part. A provider's "H100" is matched to the exact variant it sells, SXM5 or PCIe, 80 GB or 94 GB, so a PCIe price never dilutes the SXM figure. Names the matcher cannot place are logged and dropped rather than guessed.
- Bad data is quarantined, not published. A listing that lands far outside its GPU's price band is held back and flagged for review. Median, dispersion and FP8-per-dollar figures on the pricing index are calculated so that a single bad listing cannot move them.

...

A price comparison that only shows today cannot tell you whether $2.99 for an H200 is a bargain or the new normal. Since 14 July 2026 the pipeline has recorded 2,297 price points across 58 days and 101 GPUs, appending a row every time a listing changes. Each GPU pricing page plots the last 30 days with one line per provider, so you can see who cut, who held, and who quietly raised.

The index also reports a 30-day change per GPU. That figure compares the same providers' listings at both ends of the window, so a new cloud joining coverage registers as more data, not as a price move.

...

Public list prices only. Negotiated enterprise rates, reserved-capacity contracts and volume discounts are not published and are not tracked. Availability is shown where a provider publishes it, and a listed price does not guarantee capacity in the region you need. AWS and Google Cloud are the largest gaps in coverage; both publish pricing in formats that need heavier parsing and validation, and both are next on the list.

results.title: CoreWeave pricing in 2026: every GPU rate explained
highlights:
Quick Answer

CoreWeave, a GPU cloud provider, prices start at $6.16 per GPU hour for an Nvidia H100 and reaches $8.60 for a B200, sold as fixed multi-GPU nodes: an 8x H100 node lists at $49.24 per hour on demand. Spot rates run up to 60 percent below on demand, reserved contracts discount up to 60 percent, and egress is free.

...

On-demand GPU nodes run from $10.00 per hour for an 8x L40 to $68.80 for an 8x B200, with the workhorse 8x H100 node at $49.24. Every figure on the public card prices a full instance, not a chip, so the CoreWeave price you’ll actually compare against other clouds takes one extra division.

Here are CoreWeave’s North America rates as of 2026, normalized per GPU:

| GPU (instance config) | On demand, node/hr | Per GPU/hr | Spot, node/hr | Inference single GPU/hr |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nvidia HGX H100 (8x) | $49.24 | $6.16 | $19.71 | $6.16 |
| Nvidia HGX H200 (8x) | $50.44 | $6.31 | $20.93 | $6.31 |
| Nvidia HGX B200 (8x) | $68.80 | $8.60 | $34.11 | $8.60 |
| Nvidia GB200 NVL72 (4 GPU) | $42.00 | $10.50 | N/A | $10.50 |
| Nvidia HGX B300 (8x) | Contact sales | N/A | $35.84 | N/A |
| Nvidia GB300 NVL72 (4 GPU) | Contact sales | N/A | N/A | N/A |
| Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, high memory (8x) | $20.00 | $2.50 | $11.09 | $2.50 |
| Nvidia GH200 (1x) | $6.50 | $6.50 | N/A | $6.50 |
| Nvidia A100 80GB (8x) | $21.60 | $2.70 | $9.65 | $2.70 |
| Nvidia L40S (8x) | $18.00 | $2.25 | $7.88 | $2.25 |
| Nvidia L40 (8x) | $10.00 | $1.25 | $6.27 | $1.25 |

Note: GB200 and GB300 instances bundle two Grace Blackwell Superchips, four GPUs total. The inference column applies only to CoreWeave inference platform customers. European spot rates differ slightly: the H100 node runs $19.51 there versus $19.71 in North America.

...

You can buy CoreWeave compute three ways: on demand by the hour, spot at up to 60 percent off with interruption risk, and reserved capacity under negotiated multi-year contracts discounted up to 60 percent. The rate card shows the first two. The CoreWeave business model runs on the third.

No public term-rate table exists for reserved capacity. Where Google Cloud publishes its committed-use discounts in full, CoreWeave publishes a ceiling and routes you to sales. The Meta and OpenAI agreements are that tier at its extreme, and they tell you who the rate card is really for: everyone who hasn’t negotiated yet.

...

The list rate isn’t your price. Your price is the list rate divided by utilization, because a node bills at 100 percent whether your GPUs are working or waiting. CloudZero calls this the effective GPU-hour rate, and it’s the number that separates teams with defensible AI spend from teams with expensive surprises.

What utilization does to CoreWeave’s on-demand rates, in CloudZero’s arithmetic:

| Cluster utilization | H100, effective per GPU/hr | H200 | B200 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 100% (list rate) | $6.16 | $6.31 | $8.60 |
| 75% | $8.21 | $8.41 | $11.47 |
| 50% | $12.32 | $12.62 | $17.20 |
| 35% | $17.60 | $18.03 | $24.57 |

The comparison lands hard: a half-utilized H100 node on CoreWeave costs more per useful hour than a fully utilized B200. Most teams comparing providers argue about a dollar of list-rate difference while a multiple of that leaks through idle capacity, a pattern CloudZero sees constantly in GPU workload spend.

results.title: Aven Cloud vs the Largest Public Clouds | Aven Cloud
highlights:
## Quick verdict

The largest public clouds remain a strong choice when a workload is already deeply wired into their surrounding managed services. For GPU compute on its own, Aven Cloud lists on-demand H100, A100 and L40S capacity at prices meaningfully below their published list rates, billed per second with no egress fees and no minimum term — and the hourly rate you see when you launch is locked for your instance for the price-lock period (7 days on Standard). If the job is GPU-first — training, fine-tuning or inference — Aven Cloud is the more rational default on both cost and simplicity.

...

| Aspect | Aven Cloud | Largest public clouds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Billing | Per second, prepaid wallet | Typically per hour or per minute, invoiced after the fact |
| Egress fees | None | Commonly metered and billed separately |
| Minimum term | None — release anytime | Often none for on-demand, but better rates usually require a term commitment |
| Provisioning | Seconds, via dashboard or API | Minutes to hours, with more account and quota setup |
| Price visibility | One live $/GPU-hour figure per GPU | Calculators that vary by region, instance family and commitment |
| Spot/interruptible option | Yes, one field on the order call | Varies by provider and region |
| Best fit | GPU compute as the primary workload | Workloads already deep inside a specific managed-service ecosystem |

...

| Price stability | A calculator that varies by region and commitment | Can change listing to listing, day to day | Fixed for the contract term, rate rarely

...

| Provisioning time | Minutes to hours, with account and quota setup | Minutes, if a matching listing is free | Procurement plus a provisioning queue | Seconds, via dashboard or API |

...

## Pricing

These are Aven Cloud's live on-demand rates for a single GPU, compared with the public list-price range of the largest public clouds for a comparable single-GPU instance, before any reserved-capacity discount on their side.

| GPU | Aven Cloud (live) | Public cloud list price | Saving |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 SXM5 | $2.78/GPU-hour | $6.90-$12.29 | up to 77% |
| H100 PCIe | $2.52/GPU-hour | $6.98-$8.90 | up to 72% |
| A100 80GB | $0.64/GPU-hour | $3.67-$5.12 | up to 87% |
| L40S | $0.94/GPU-hour | $1.86 | up to 49% |

Billing integrity is enforced by a continuous reconciliation loop that checks real provider state against what your account is charged for, so capacity you released is never billed by mistake. On-demand prices also adjust continuously with supply and demand, but the rate shown when you order is locked in for you for the length of your price lock (7 days on Standard), so the number in the table above won't move under you mid-decision. See security for details.

Prices are per GPU, per hour, in USD, and refresh continuously — see the full breakdown on pricing or browse each GPU's own page, starting with H100 SXM5. Need to cut the bill further? An interruptible spot instance reduces the same on-demand rate again for workloads that can tolerate a reclaim.

## Monthly cost at 24/7

Running a GPU around the clock for a full month is the case where the hourly gap adds up the most. At Aven Cloud's on-demand rate, an H100 SXM5 held 24/7 for a month comes to $2029.40 — and that figure is a ceiling, not a commitment. Stop the instance the moment the job is done and billing stops with it, down to the second; there is no reserved-instance paperwork and no multi-year commitment required to see that number.

| GPU | Monthly at 24/7 (on-demand) |

| H100 SXM5 | $2029.40 |
| A100 80GB | $467.20 |
| L40S | $686.20 |

results.title: H100 Rents Give Back Nvidia's 22% Bounce
highlights:
Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang on September 8 amplified a chart showing H100 rentals at $3.28 an hour, up 22% in a month. The same Ornn index’s settled H100 print of $2.92 on September 24 was down 1.8% over 30 days from $2.97.

That 17-day drop from $3.28 to $2.92 is 11%, and it landed while Nvidia still posted $96.2 billion quarterly revenue and a market value near $5.41 trillion. A noisy neocloud tape is a thin way to close a fight about how Big Tech books GPU lives.

...

Ornn, the compute-market firm behind the OCPI-H100, posted on September 7 that the H100 was “a three-year-old training chip” whose rental price was up 22% on the month, to $3.28 an hour. Huang quoted the tape the next day.

...

The settled daily series on Ornn’s public page never treated that $3.28 hour as a durable level. By September 24 the index was $2.92 per GPU-hour, or $70.02 per GPU-day and about $2,100.60 per GPU-month, after a 4.3% one-day drop from $3.05. The seven-day change was still +2.4%. The 30-day change was not.

...

OCPI-H100 is not a hyperscaler list price and not a used-chip bid. Ornn Data LLC publishes it as a settlement-style benchmark of on-demand H100 SXM rentals, listed on Bloomberg and built as a volume-weighted winsorized mean of executed trades over a rolling one-hour window, then settled once a trading day at 4:00 p.m. ET.

...

The rental tape already prices that ladder. On September 24, Ornn’s settled prints were $2.92 for H100 SXM, $5.16 for H200, $8.01 for B200, and $1.02 for A100 SXM4. An H100 hour cleared at 36% of a B200 hour, or about 2.7 times cheaper on a raw GPU-hour, before anyone adjusts for tokens per watt.

SETTLED OCPI PRINTS ON SEPTEMBER 24

| GPU | Index ($/GPU-hr) | Share of a B200 hour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| B200 | $8.01 | 100% |
| H200 | $5.16 | 64% |
| H100 SXM | $2.92 | 36% |
| A100 SXM4 | $1.02 | 13% |

results.title: Nvidia Blackwell Demand Sent Nebius Auction Prices 20% Higher - Passport to Wall Street
highlights:
Artificial intelligence infrastructure companies have spent the past two years raising prices as demand for high-end GPUs outpaced supply. Nebius Group N.V. (NBIS ) just revealed that even repeated price hikes weren't enough.

Instead, the company turned to auctions-and customers voluntarily paid another 15% to 20% above its previous highest prices to secure guaranteed access to Nvidia Corp's (NVDA ) Blackwell-powered AI compute.

...

Speaking about the company's latest pricing experiment at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference 2026, Nebius founder and CEO Arkady Volozh said traditional price increases failed to balance supply and demand.

"When you have this imbalance between demand and supply, the best price discovery mechanism is something like an auction," Volozh said.

The company first tried manually raising prices, but demand remained resilient. "We tried to do it manually first to raise the prices. It didn't help. The demand is still there," he said.

That prompted Nebius to test an auction for access to Blackwell compute capacity. The result surprised even the company.

"We achieved results when we got 15%, 20% higher price than we ever sold before, after all our price raises," Volozh said.

...

Rather than simply charging a fixed rate for Nvidia Blackwell compute, Nebius allowed customers to bid for guaranteed capacity. According to Volozh, the winning customers were satisfied because the auction eliminated uncertainty over whether they would receive the computing resources they needed.

results.title: H100 GPU Rental Rates Climb to $3.28/hr in 2026 Despite Chip Age · The Information Machine
highlights:
The full picture

H100 one-year contract rental rates rose roughly 40% between October 2025 ($1.70/hr) and July 2026 (~$2.80/hr), with spot prices reaching $3.28/hr in September 2026 per the Ornn index. Marketplace median rates sit at $3.38/hr, with the cheapest tracked rate at $1.49/hr on Vast.ai. The price increase occurred even after Nvidia's Blackwell generation shipped, contrary to standard hardware depreciation patterns. The primary demand driver is AI inference for reasoning and agentic workloads, which consume far more tokens per request than simple chat. Supply constraints include TSMC CoWoS packaging capacity, HBM memory output, and 36-52 week lead times against a roughly 3.6 million unit industry backlog; HBM costs rose around 30% in Q4 2025. AWS raised H200 instance prices 15% in January 2026. Newer chips command higher rates: the H200 runs $3.59-$4.59/hr, the B200 $5.63-$8.64/hr, while AMD MI300X undercuts Nvidia equivalents at as low as $1.85/hr on Vultr. H100 rates are projected to drift toward $1/hr by mid-2027 as B200 absorbs premium demand, following the depreciation curve the A100 followed.

results.title: A four year old chip is now more expensive to rent than when it was brand new and that shows you the demand for compute (Save this). | Milk Road
highlights:
The H100 launched in 2023 and should be obsolete by now but instead, its one year rental contract price climbed from a low of $1.70/hr in October 2025 to roughly $2.35/hr by March 2026, a nearly 40% move in five months.

The chart shows that climb continuing through July 2026, back near $2.80/hr, which is roughly where the chip priced in early 2024.

Spot pricing went further, with the Ornn index putting H100 rentals at $3.28/hr in September 2026, up 22% in a single month.

This breaks the normal rules of hardware because every depreciation model assumes older chips lose value once a new generation arrives, yet Blackwell shipped and the H100 got more expensive anyway.

The bottleneck has essentially moved from chips to everything around them.

On demand capacity has been effectively sold out across GPU types, with buyers refusing to release instances back into the pool even after price hikes.

H100 nodes carry 36 to 52 week lead times against an industry backlog of roughly 3.6 million units.

The real constraint is TSMC CoWoS packaging and HBM output, neither of which expands quickly and HBM costs alone rose about 30% in Q4 2025.

Pricing power has flipped to the sellers in a way with no modern precedent.

AWS raised H200 instance prices 15% in January 2026, its first GPU price increase in roughly two decades.

Microsoft, Google, Meta and Amazon placed multi billion dollar forward orders that consumed most of Nvidia's allocation through 2026 and into 2027, pulling inventory off the market before it ever reaches smaller buyers.

results.title: Nebius Stock Is Actually Cheap (NASDAQ:NBIS) | Seeking Alpha
highlights:
## Summary

- NBIS is signing multiyear AI-cloud contracts exceeding $1 billion on average, supported by strong demand for GPU capacity and attractive contract economics.
- Customer prepayments cover 50% to 60% of associated capacity capex, improving cash conversion and reducing capital payback periods.
- Nebius charges $7.15 per hour for B200 capacity, above the broader market benchmark, while short-duration capacity can earn materially higher revenue per megawatt of capacity.
- Remaining performance obligations reached $37.5B, with $13.5B expected to convert into revenue within 2 years, and management is targeting $8B of year-end ARR.
- NBIS trades above peers on forward revenue multiples, but its implied long-term revenue growth requirement remains well below the expected revenue projections.
